# Hand out ids in blocks of 1,000 from Redis

> [`IdLease`](share-short-links.md) leases a block of 1,000 sequential IDs from Redis with one call, then hands them out from memory to reduce database pressure.

_Part of [Creating and resolving share links](share-short-links.md)_

When you create a short link, you need a unique ID to scramble into a short code. Asking Redis for each ID would be slow. [`IdLease`](share-short-links.md) solves this with a ticket-server pattern: it leases a block of 1,000 IDs with one Redis call, hands them out from memory, and only fetches the next block when this one runs out. Every server instance does this independently without coordinating with the others. If a server crashes before using its entire batch, those IDs are skipped—which is harmless. The public API is just `nextId()`, which returns the next ID from the current batch, blocking only when a new batch needs to be leased from Redis. This lives in the marketing infra layer as part of [Creating and resolving share links](share-short-links.md), feeding sequential IDs to the [Feistel scrambler](feistel-code-scrambler.md) that turns them into random-looking codes.

**Look at:** [`IdLease` in id-lease.ts](../../../../packages/backend/libs/domains/marketing/infra/id-lease.ts#L9)

## What it touches

| Kind | Name | How |
|---|---|---|
| cache | `Redis counter (key parameter)` | Incremented via INCRBY by `blockSize` (default 1,000) to atomically allocate ID ranges; each instance uses the returned value to determine its block |

## Watch out

- The Redis INCRBY returns the value after increment; the code calculates the block start as `end - blockSize + 1` to claim the returned value and its 999 predecessors
- Multiple [`IdLease`](share-short-links.md) instances sharing the same Redis key will interfere with each other—use a unique key per instance or feature
- The `pending` promise deduplicates concurrent lease() calls; if multiple `nextId`() requests arrive during a lease, they all wait for the same Redis round-trip
- ID sequence gaps from crashed instances are expected and harmless; don't add logic to fill them
